title: One phrase, two durations
subtitle: Locate the change before interpreting its effect.
summary: Compare two generated versions of an original eight-beat rhythmic phrase. Keep onset positions fixed, inspect short and sustained tone envelopes, then explore tempo without confusing beats with seconds.
audience: Beginners; no notation or craft experience required.
scope: Generated sine-tone rhythm, not a human percussion recording. Event tables support structural comparison; they do not reproduce hearing or establish a universal emotional effect.

passages.title: Describe a choice, then explain a response
passages.text: Tempo, dynamics and articulation offer ways to compare musical choices and discuss how listeners interpret them. An observation about timing is different from an interpretation of expressive effect.
passages.context: Original instructional paraphrase. No Carnegie repertoire or media is used; the source does not validate this generated stimulus or prescribe one emotion for a particular sound.

claims.text: At the same tempo, the two generated versions share onset positions, sine frequency and peak gain while their tone-envelope lengths differ.
claims.qualification: This is a property of the authored event/synthesis specification, not a claim of equal perceived loudness, energy or timbre.

claims.text: A duration difference can support more than one reasoned expressive interpretation.
claims.qualification: Perceptibility, musical usefulness and learner responses have not been evaluated by a performer or participant.

context: The span is eight quarter-note beats, shown as two groups of four in this Western beat-grid exercise. There are nine tone events; eight beats does not mean eight sounds. Beat offsets start at zero; the first event is displayed as beat 1.

The original onset offsets are 0, 1, 1.5, 2.5, 3, 4, 5.5, 6 and 7 beats. Short tones last 0.12 beat and sustained tones 0.42 beat. Neither version connects every adjacent tone, so sustained is not labeled legato.
For a beat offset b and tempo T, elapsed seconds = b × 60 / T. Tone lengths scale with beats when tempo changes; oscillator frequency stays 440 Hz. Attack and release remain 5 ms and 15 ms.
Equal oscillator settings and peak gain are controlled signal parameters, not equal perceived loudness, timbre or signal energy. The master-volume control is not loudness normalization.

The sound is mono, generated from a sine formula with smooth attack/release and no third-party samples. The arrangement and diagrams are Codex-assisted original work for this pilot; no human composer or performer is invented.

Select a replay region and start playback yourself. Version, tempo or region changes stop the current sound. Pause preserves an approximate beat cursor; shared cursors do not establish what another person heard.

This is a local draft. A performer/educator, actual learner/accessibility observations and final release terms remain open. The no-audio event task supports structure and interpretation, not an identical sensory experience.

activity.transfer: Keep the onset pattern but compare a slower tempo with longer tones. Cite an event and its beat/second values, identify which variables changed, then offer two possible listener responses and explain what actual observation would test them.
rubric: Locate evidence by event ID and beat offset; include seconds at the chosen tempo.
Separate onset, tone length, gap, frequency and peak gain from perceived loudness or expressive character.
Give two reasoned interpretations without treating a mood label as an answer key.
Distinguish generated signal, human performance and listener evidence.
Explain what the visual/no-audio route can establish and what it cannot.
